analysis.one_liner: Greatly raises tax-free health savings account limits and lets new pools sell group health plans.
analysis.headline: Senator Rand Paul introduced the bill on December 4, 2025; it has zero cosponsors and no committee action since referral, so it has not received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let anyone put much more money into a health savings account — tying the annual limit to the same cap as 401(k)-style plans — and would drop the rule that you must be enrolled in a high-deductible insurance plan to contribute. HSA dollars could then pay for health insurance premiums, direct primary care fees, vitamins, dietary supplements, gym memberships, and fitness trackers, and the accounts would get bankruptcy protection like retirement funds. A second title would let member-run "health marketplace pools" be treated as employers under federal benefits law so they can offer group health plans, including plans that cover only prescription drugs.
analysis.who_benefits: Households with cash to save — especially higher earners, who get the largest tax deductions for the biggest contributions — plus self-employed people and small firms that could join a pool to buy group-rate coverage. Insurers, direct primary care practices, and the vitamin, supplement, gym, and fitness-tracker businesses also gain a new stream of pre-tax customer spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Savers who can shelter income, especially high earners

how_it_helps.text: Removes the requirement that a person be enrolled in a high-deductible health plan to contribute to an HSA, by striking the eligibility subsections of the tax code's HSA provision.
Raises the annual HSA contribution limit to the same cap that applies to 401(k)-style employee plans, with an additional catch-up amount for people 50 and older.
Allows HSA funds to pay for health insurance premiums and for direct primary care service arrangements, and extends qualified-expense treatment to a dependent child up to age 27.
Allows HSA funds to be spent on vitamins, dietary supplements, gym memberships, and wearable fitness trackers as 'qualified wellness expenses.'
Gives health savings accounts the same protection from creditors in bankruptcy that retirement accounts receive.
Lets medical expenses incurred in the year an account is opened (or the preceding year, under a narrow rule) count as qualified expenses, so new account holders are not penalized for timing.

Amends federal benefits law so that an entity meeting the requirements is deemed an 'employer' and can offer group health plans — including drug-only coverage 'notwithstanding any other provision of law' — to its members and their employers' employees.
Bars health marketplace pools from conditioning membership on health status and requires enrollment rules applied consistently to all members.

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury bears the revenue cost of larger deductions and of subsidized spending on items like gym memberships and vitamins, since the bill text contains no funding offsets. If pool plans offer thin drug-only coverage, members with expensive conditions could end up with worse protection, and ERISA treatment can displace some state insurance rules that would otherwise apply.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal revenue; sicker members of pool plans

drawbacks.text: The tax benefit scales with income and savings capacity: households able to shelter the largest contributions capture the biggest deductions, so the revenue cost concentrates its benefit at the top while everyone shares the deficit cost.

Allowing HSA money to pay insurance premiums converts a savings account into a pre-tax funnel for premiums, shrinking the account balance available for actual medical bills and deepening the subsidy for people who already have coverage.
Spending HSA dollars on vitamins, supplements, gym memberships, and fitness trackers subsidizes purchases of debatable medical value and adds revenue cost with no corresponding health guarantee.

Health marketplace pools may offer coverage where a prescription or nonprescription drug plan is the only benefit, 'notwithstanding any other provision of law,' which could leave members with chronic conditions carrying more of their own drug costs.
The bill text contains no revenue offsets to pay for the expanded deductions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people who can save, the bill is a real, if regressive, tax benefit: dropping the high-deductible-plan requirement opens HSAs to millions of workers with ordinary insurance, and letting savings cover premiums and family rollovers adds flexibility. But the largest deductions flow to those who can shelter the most, the wellness-expansion provisions reward spending that is not clearly medical, and the pool title's allowance for drug-only plans and its lack of revenue offsets are genuine design weaknesses an honest supporter would have to acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on December 4, 2025, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing or vote so far.

narrative.text: Senator Rand Paul introduced S. 3362 in the Senate on December 4, 2025, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance.
The bill has zero cosponsors, according to the Congress.gov cosponsor list.
No further action beyond the referral appears in the bill's action history, and the Congress remains in session until January 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one yet; the bill has only been referred to committee and nothing about the status quo has changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; nothing has changed

for.name: Sen. Rand Paul
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee as its sole sponsor.

sides.party_line_note: One Republican introduced the bill and no one from either party has signed on or opposed it on the record.

industries.note: HSA dollars could pay premiums directly, giving insurers a steadier stream of pre-tax revenue and making customers less price-sensitive; insurers may also contract with the new marketplace pools. Drug-only pool plans, however, could shift costs onto members with expensive conditions.

Raising the contribution limit to the 401(k)-style cap creates a much larger tax shelter for those able to contribute the maximum, with the biggest deductions going to the highest earners and the revenue cost shared by all taxpayers.

industries.industry: Vitamin, supplement, gym, and fitness-tracker businesses
industries.note: The bill designates their products as tax-advantaged 'qualified wellness expenses' purchasable with HSA funds, creating a new pre-tax customer base.
HSA funds could pay direct primary care membership fees, opening a pre-tax payment channel for these practices.

The marketplace-pool title lets member-run pools offer group health coverage — including to members' employees — potentially at better rates than individuals can buy on their own, though plan quality would vary.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and no committee action two sessions into the 119th Congress, the bill is unlikely to receive a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee; most single-sponsor bills referred to committee never advance.
